name: Pangolin (pgl)
baseline: CGAL 6.1.2 (EPECK and EPICK kernels): Delaunay_triangulation_2, Kd_tree, AABB_tree, convex_hull_2, Arrangement_2, Boolean_set_operations_2, minkowski_sum_2 and others
workload: Wall-clock run time of about 20 planar computational-geometry problems (Delaunay triangulation, point/segment search, convex hull, segment intersection, arrangements, polygon unions, Minkowski sum, visibility), pgl vs CGAL on identical integer-coordinate inputs, sizes up to the benchmark's range, including Salzburg polygon datasets.
claimed_speedup: Ratios are pgl time / CGAL time, median over sizes (below 1 = pgl faster). int/EPICK: count points in triangle 0.21x (0.14-0.24), segment search count in triangle 0.21x, segment intersection 0.35x, convex hull 0.51x, segment search count in rectangle 0.51x. ERational/EPECK: regularized union of triangles 0.23x, arrangement point-location query 0.46x, segment intersection 0.55x, arrangement point-location build 0.61x. CGAL is faster elsewhere: Delaunay triangulation (pgl 1.7x slower int/EPICK, 2.6x slower ERational/EPECK), convex hull ERational 1.8x slower, Minkowski sum 1.7x slower. Overall range on ERational/EPECK: CGAL 2.6x faster to pgl 4.4x faster; on int/EPICK: CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl 4.8x faster.
hardware: Two machines, one run each (CPU models not named on the cited page); ratios averaged over the machines
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, 2D plane only; exact predicates on integer coordinates, ERational for exact constructions; much smaller feature set than CGAL; library chooses algorithms for the user; predicates return bool.
caveats: First-party benchmark. The page itself states pgl is tuned against this benchmark, that some rows favour pgl by construction (CGAL ships no triangle query for Kd_tree so the baseline wrote one), and that orthogonal range counting is deliberately omitted. Results are genuinely mixed: CGAL wins Delaunay, Minkowski sum and several build rows. CPU models and per-machine numbers are not on the page; the online benchmark charts (github.io) were not opened. Very new repo with 6 stars.

name: Indexicon R-tree
workload: R-tree insertion time and range-query time versus Boost's R-tree for node capacities 32-512 on six spatial datasets (MARINE, MIAMI, OSM, TAXIS, TIGER, TORONTO).
claimed_speedup: README shows charts only (no table). Approximate values read off the README charts: insertion on MARINE at capacity 512 about 31.8 s (Boost) vs about 25 s (Indexicon), roughly 20% faster; range query on MARINE at capacity 32 about 425 ms vs about 280 ms (roughly 34% faster); TORONTO capacity 32 about 38.5 ms vs about 30.5 ms; near parity on MIAMI and TIGER at some capacities (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Single-header C++17 R-tree, quad-tree, MX-CIF quad-tree, oct-tree and KD-tree; point and MBB data; top-down packing, R* insertion, deletion with orphan reinsertion.
caveats: Own benchmark against Boost only, shown as chart images; compiler, flags and CPU are not on the README and the comprehensive results are in an arXiv preprint (2606.04676) that could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked). Which Boost balancing algorithm (linear, quadratic, rstar) was used is not stated. Gains are modest (about 10-35%) and some configurations are at parity. Repo created 2026-05.

name: PH-tree (phtree-cpp)
baseline: Boost.Geometry R-tree (boost::geometry::index::rtree); libspatialindex R-tree also measured
workload: 3D points and boxes, CUBE (uniform) and CLUSTER datasets, 1K to 1M entries: insert, window query (about 3-15 results per query) and kNN, PH-tree vs Boost R-tree vs libspatialindex vs MCXME PH-tree.
claimed_speedup: Insert at 1M entries (CUBE / CLUSTER): points PhTreeMM 2.79M/s vs BoostRT 500k/s and 3.97M/s vs 781k/s (about 5.6x and 5.1x, derived from page data); boxes PhTree3D 1.44M/s vs BoostRT 406k/s and 3.18M/s vs 573k/s (about 3.5x and 5.6x, derived); libspatialindex 104k/s and 111k/s on points. Window queries are mixed: point data at 1M, PhTree3D 314k q/s vs BoostRT 364k q/s on CUBE (Boost 1.16x faster) and 1.35M q/s vs 990k q/s on CLUSTER (PH-tree 1.36x faster); box data at 1M on CUBE, PhTree3D 56.3k q/s vs BoostRT 263.6k q/s (Boost about 4.7x faster). kNN results in the perf repo mostly favour Boost.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.1 (insert benchmark, 2023-02-01) and Clang 14.0.0 (kNN benchmark, 2023-03-09); flags not stated (bazel --config=benchmark)
hardware: 8 x 4600 MHz CPU, L3 12 MiB (model not named in the result files)
tradeoffs: Z-order PH-tree: very fast insert/erase/relocate, scales to millions of entries and higher dimensions; not efficient when queries return 1000+ results; header-only C++17; coordinates go through converters; multimap variants exist.
caveats: Benchmark written by the PH-tree author; the benchmark page notes Boost RT was driven with std::array coordinates (small slowdown), libspatialindex wrapper uses a buffering hack and has an unexplained web-dataset result bug. The win is insertion; queries and kNN are mixed or favour Boost's R-tree. Fork of Improbable's unmaintained original (maintained by the original PH-tree developer). CPU model and compiler flags missing, so not tier A.

name: Boost.Geometry.Index R-tree
baseline: libspatialindex R-tree (also SQLite3 R*Tree extension in the file-backed test)
workload: Third-party file-backed test: insert and query boxes (100 to 100,000) with libspatialindex, SQLite3 R*Tree and Boost.Geometry (memory-mapped file). Boost authors' test: 1,000,000 random boxes loaded by linear/quadratic/R* iteration or bulk loading, then 100,000 intersection queries, vs libspatialindex.
claimed_speedup: cmpute suite (Ubuntu 20.04 WSL2): 100,000 boxes insertion 0.195 ms/box (Boost) vs 0.876 ms/box (libspatialindex) and 0.443 ms/box (SQLite R*Tree), i.e. about 4.5x and 2.3x (derived from page data); query at 10,000 boxes 0.0217 ms/box vs 0.2852 and 0.6142 (about 13x and 28x, derived); file size after shrink 6.19 MB vs 25.8 MB and 8.5 MB. mloskot suite (values read off README charts, approximate): bulk-loaded R* 1M objects about 1.1 s (bgi) vs about 5.5 s (libspatialindex STR); 100K intersection queries on the bulk-loaded tree about 0.05-0.12 s vs about 2-6 s; iterative R* load of 1M objects about 3-13 s vs about 25-108 s depending on node capacity.
compiler_and_flags: mloskot: Visual C++ 11.0 (Visual Studio 2012) 32-bit build, flags not stated; cmpute: not stated
hardware: mloskot: Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.10GHz, 16 GB RAM, Windows 7; cmpute: Ubuntu 20.04 on WSL2, CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only, requires Boost headers; compile-time or run-time node parameters; bulk loading; persistent storage only through memory-mapped files, which are not dynamically sized.
caveats: Boost.Geometry is itself one of this category's named incumbents, so this entry only claims its R-tree beats libspatialindex and SQLite R*Tree. The cmpute repo is archived (last commit 2021-04-22), has no license file, 2 stars, and does not state compiler, flags or CPU; the mloskot repo (last commit 2019-07-07, authors include a Boost.Geometry.Index author) calls itself a non-academic first prototype with possible bugs. The cmpute note says mmap storage is not strictly file-based. Old library versions; the mloskot numbers are chart read-offs. Query checksums in the cmpute logs differ between libraries, so result equality was not demonstrated.

name: Contour-Coherent Hausdorff Distance
workload: Exact discrete Hausdorff distance between all pairs of ordered image contours (21 related walking silhouettes, 210 pair evaluations), total package time.
claimed_speedup: Walking silhouettes: 50.48 ms total package (0.240 ms per HD) vs Boost discrete Hausdorff 12382.56 ms (58.96 ms per HD), stated as approximately 245x faster; also 16.3x faster than brute force with shuffling and 88.9x faster than brute force with early stop. Boost was only run on this package; on unrelated shape sets (Kimia216) the method is only about equal to shuffled brute force.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release preset (x64-release, MSVC / GCC via Ninja); optimization flags not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only, dependency-free; exact result; custom point types and L2/L1/Chebyshev policies; relies on ordered, coherent contours; worst case still O(n*m).
caveats: First-party benchmark, hardware not stated. The speedup exploits contour ordering that Boost's general function does not use, so it is a specialised-input comparison; Boost is only reported on the walking-silhouette package. Very new repo (created 2026-05) with 1 star. README also lists an OpenCV FLANN kd-tree baseline.

name: CavalierContours
baseline: Clipper (ClipperLib polygon offsetting, Angus Johnson, original Clipper)
workload: Repeated inward and outward offsetting (rounded joins) of 2D polylines with arcs: square, circle, rounded rectangle, two small profiles and pathological circles of N alternating half-circle arcs; Clipper given arcs approximated at 1e-2 or 1e-3.
claimed_speedup: Arcs approximated for both (1e-2): 3.5x faster on the square (0.21 vs 0.72 ms), 4.0x on PathologicalProfile1/100 (336.37 vs 1347.09 ms), but slower on BM_Profile1 (0.7x) and BM_Profile2 (0.9x). Arcs kept exactly vs Clipper at 1e-2: 76.4x on the circle (0.12 vs 9.47 ms), 84.9x on PathologicalProfile1/10 (1.61 vs 136.46 ms), 15.8x on PathologicalProfile1/100 (85.10 vs 1347.09 ms). Against Clipper at 1e-3: up to 494.7x on the circle and 861.0x on PathologicalProfile1/10.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2019 19.24.28314 targeting 64-bit (MinGW 7.3 64-bit gave similar results); optimization flags not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only C++14 with C API; 2D polylines with constant-radius arcs; offset, boolean ops, winding number and area; packed Hilbert R-tree spatial index; absolute float thresholds so inputs may need rescaling.
caveats: First-party benchmark from about 2019-2020 hardware; benchmark code is in a separate dev repo (CavalierContoursDev) that was not opened. Most of the large ratios come from keeping arcs exact instead of approximating them, which is a different representation from Clipper's; the arcs-approximated comparison is much closer and loses on two profiles. Author says the C++ version is no longer maintained (a Rust version replaces it). Clipper version not named.

name: Delaunay32
baseline: Triangle 1.6 (also CDT 1.4.5, delaunator-cpp c1521f6 and Fade2D 2.17.3; CGAL not compared)
workload: 2D Delaunay triangulation of one million unique, unconstrained signed 32-bit integer points, triangle-only output.
claimed_speedup: Delaunay32 45.4 ms at 8 threads and 131.6 ms single-threaded vs Fade2D 235.2 ms (automatic threads) / 314.1 ms (1 thread), delaunator-cpp 542.0 ms, Triangle 1.6 584.0 ms, CDT 1.4.5 988.7 ms; README relative runtimes 1.0x, 2.9x, 5.2x, 6.9x, 11.9x, 12.9x, 21.8x. Single-thread Delaunay32 vs Triangle about 4.4x and vs CDT about 7.5x (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Signed 32-bit integer coordinates only (floats go through an explicit quantize step); exact integer predicates; serial or shared-memory parallel; constraints and polygon domains with holes; MIT, no third-party source dependencies; WebAssembly build exists.
caveats: First-party README table for one distribution and size; compiler, flags and competitor build settings are not stated; competitors take floating-point input while Delaunay32 requires integer input (input conversion excluded). Fade2D is commercial. CGAL, the named incumbent, is not in the comparison. Repo created 2026-07-26.

name: alpha-wrap (CGAL-free Alpha Wrapping)
workload: Alpha wrapping with offset of triangle soups (bundled meshes, a 100k-triangle sphere and a 236k-triangle Actaeon statue, alpha = diag/30), compared with the CGAL reference build for speed, topology and Hausdorff distance.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Speed: competitive to faster (ours ~2x faster on most inputs in this GMP-free CGAL environment)'. Same page: face count 0.6-1.0x CGAL's, symmetric Hausdorff distance to the CGAL wrap 0.1%-3.4% of the bbox diagonal. No per-model timing table.
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for the comparison build (RelWithDebInfo for the default build); optimization flags and compiler not stated
tradeoffs: Clean-room implementation of the TOG 2022 algorithm; only dependency is Shewchuk's public-domain predicates (no CGAL, no GPL); Python bindings via nanobind; coarser output (0.6-1.0x faces) and small geometric deviations from CGAL's wrap.
caveats: One summary sentence with no timing table; the CGAL reference is built without GMP, which makes CGAL slower than a typical install; hardware and compiler unstated; very new repo, and the commit history shows AI co-authorship. Not an independent measurement.

name: PicoTree
baseline: nanoflann v1.7.1 (also OpenCV FLANN 4.11.0, SciPy KDTree, scikit-learn KDTree, pykdtree)
workload: Single-threaded kd-tree build over a 7,733,372-point LiDAR cloud and nearest-neighbour (knn=1) queries with a second 7,200,863-point cloud, max_leaf_size=10.
claimed_speedup: Build 0.54 s vs nanoflann 1.42 s (2.6x, derived from page data) and OpenCV FLANN 0.99 s; knn query 1.13 s vs nanoflann 1.40 s (1.2x, derived) and OpenCV FLANN 2.30 s. Python: knn 1.64 s vs SciPy KDTree 212.04 s, scikit-learn 11.90 s, pykdtree 2.95 s; Python build 0.54 s vs pykdtree 0.43 s (pykdtree faster).

tradeoffs: Header-only C++ kd-tree with Python bindings; Eigen, OpenCV and custom point types; sliding-midpoint build; range and knn search.
caveats: Author's own benchmark on one LiDAR dataset. docs/benchmark.md says nanoflann's build regressed by about 90% in v1.5.0, which inflates the build gap against nanoflann v1.7.1; the detailed C++ comparison is plots only. Compiler and flags for the README table are not stated. nanoflann is not a listed incumbent for this category.

name: picoflann
workload: Exact kd-tree index build, knn and radius search on a small point set (README heading says 10,000 2D points, the speed-up block says 3D points).
claimed_speedup: Index building: 1.46x faster than nanoflann, 1.73x faster than OpenCV FLANN. Knn: 4.14x faster than nanoflann, 1.8x faster than OpenCV FLANN. Radius search: 1.25x faster than nanoflann, 3.21x faster than OpenCV FLANN.
stars_or_usage: 22 stars; part of the ucoslam project
tradeoffs: Minimal header-only exact kd-tree search with a small adapter API; picoflann2.h added in 2026; no license file in the repo.
caveats: First-party README with no hardware, compiler, flags or k stated, and an internal inconsistency (10,000 2D points vs 'Speed up in 3D points'). An independent robotics benchmark (LimHyungTae/OpenFLANN, 200,000 points, 1,000 repeats, charts) found nanoflann faster at K=1 (0.00215 ms vs 0.00242 ms per search) and picoflann much faster at K=5000 (0.84 ms vs 8.36 ms), so the 4.14x knn figure does not hold across K. No LICENSE file found in the repo, so code must be treated as reference only. nanoflann is not a listed incumbent here.

name: madmann91/bvh
baseline: nanort and Fast-BVH (Embree 3.13 also compared and is faster)
workload: BVH build time and primary-ray render time (1 spp at 720p) on a Blend Swap scene, comparing BVH v2 presets with Embree 3.13, nanort and Fast-BVH.
claimed_speedup: Values read off the README chart (approximate): BVH v2 (medium) builds in about 150 ms and renders in about 275 ms vs nanort about 360 ms build / 645 ms render and Fast-BVH about 460 ms build / 1225 ms render (about 2.3x and 4.5x faster render, derived from page data); Embree 3.13 is faster than all BVH presets (about 70 ms build, 170 ms render).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 BVH construction and traversal, multiple builders (sweep SAH, binned SAH, multithreaded), C API, serialization; does not reach Embree's speed.
caveats: Numbers are only in a chart image: no CPU, compiler, flags, thread count or scene size stated. It beats the simple libraries (nanort, Fast-BVH) but not the real incumbent Embree. Ray tracing BVH is only loosely within geometry-spatial; none of this category's named baselines (Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS, R-trees) is compared.
